quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on specific volume, the cylinder model and what the diameter formulas assume.

questions.q: What does specific volume (v) of a yarn mean?
options: Volume in cm³ occupied by one gram of yarn
Weight in grams of one cm³ of yarn
Length of yarn in one gram
Diameter of the yarn in mm
questions.explain: Specific volume is cm³ per gram, the reciprocal of density; the lecture takes about 1.1 cm³/g for a cotton yarn in cloth. Grams per cm³ would be the density.

questions.q: What value of specific volume does the lecture suggest for a cotton yarn in cloth?
questions.explain: About 1.1 cm³/g. 1.54 is close to the density of cotton fibre itself (g/cm³) and 26.7 is the constant in the tex formula.

questions.q: The derivation models the yarn as a
options: Solid cylinder of uniform specific volume
questions.explain: One metre of yarn is treated as a solid cylinder whose volume π d² l ÷ 4 equals its mass times its specific volume.

questions.q: One metre of a yarn of N tex weighs
questions.explain: Tex is grams per 1,000 m, so one metre weighs N ÷ 1,000 g. 1,000 ÷ N would be metres per gram.

questions.q: The formula d (mm) = √tex ÷ 26.7 already has the specific volume of about 1.1 cm³/g built into the constant.
questions.explain: The 26.7 comes from evaluating √(4 v ÷ (1000 π l)) with v ≈ 1.1 and l = 100 cm; a different specific volume would give a different constant.

questions.q: Why does the lecture call the yarn diameter the number behind every cover and crimp calculation?
options: Because cover factor and crimp both depend on how much space each yarn takes up
Because it sets the yarn count
Because it fixes the loom speed
questions.explain: Cover is the fraction of the cloth area filled by yarn and crimp is the bending of one yarn around another; both are governed by the yarn's thickness.

questions.q: Which statement about real cotton yarns in cloth does the lecture make?
options: They are flattened and cover more than the circular model predicts
They are thinner than the model predicts
Their diameter does not depend on count
questions.explain: In cloth the yarns are pressed flat at the interlacings, so the actual cover is greater than a circular cross-section would give.

questions.q: A yarn with a higher specific volume is denser and therefore thinner for the same count.
questions.explain: Higher specific volume means more cm³ per gram, i.e. a bulkier, less dense yarn, which is thicker for the same tex — the opposite of the statement.

questions.q: In the formula d = √(4 v N ÷ (1000 π l)), what is l?
options: The yarn length in cm, taken as 100 cm (one metre)
questions.explain: The derivation uses one metre of yarn, so l = 100 cm; N is the count in tex and v the specific volume.

questions.q: Which figure is the lecture's quick estimate of the maximum cover factor per direction?
questions.explain: 126 Ne 20 yarns touching fill an inch; 126 ÷ √20 ≈ 28, which is the ceiling for cover factor in one direction. 126 is the thread count, not the cover factor.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The three diameter formulas, what varies with what, and how count, specific volume and diameter move together.

questions.q: Which formula gives the diameter in mm from the English cotton count?
questions.explain: d (mm) = 0.9 ÷ √Ne. A finer (higher) Ne gives a thinner yarn, so Ne must be in the denominator; the √tex ÷ 26.7 form is for tex.

questions.q: If the tex of a yarn is quadrupled, its diameter
questions.explain: Diameter is proportional to √tex, so √4 = 2: the diameter doubles. Quadrupling would require d ∝ tex.

questions.q: If the Ne count doubles (the yarn becomes finer), the diameter is multiplied by
questions.explain: d ∝ 1 ÷ √Ne, so doubling Ne divides d by √2 (about 0.71). Halving would need a fourfold rise in Ne.

questions.q: Changing the specific volume from 1.1 to 1.0 cm³/g makes the calculated diameter
questions.explain: d ∝ √v, and √(1.0 ÷ 1.1) ≈ 0.953, so the yarn is about 5 % thinner, as the lecture states. The 10 % change in v is halved by the square root.

questions.q: The number of threads per inch that can lie touching is 25.4 divided by the diameter in mm.
questions.explain: There are 25.4 mm in an inch, so 25.4 ÷ d yarns of diameter d fit side by side, exactly as the worksheet row computes.

questions.q: The inch version of the formula is d (in) ≈ 1 ÷ (28 √Ne). Where does the 28 come from?
questions.explain: 0.9 mm ÷ √Ne converted to inches is (0.9 ÷ 25.4) ÷ √Ne = 1 ÷ (28.2 √Ne).

questions.q: In the worksheet the three diameter rows for an Ne 20 yarn (0.203, 0.204 and 0.201 mm) differ slightly because
options: They use different rounding of the same cylinder model and constants
The specific volume of 1.1 is wrong
questions.explain: All three come from the same model; the small differences are rounding in the constants 26.7 and 0.9 and in the conversion from Ne to tex.

questions.q: The maximum cover factor per direction (about 28) is obtained as
questions.explain: Cover factor = threads per inch ÷ √Ne; with the touching thread count 25.4 ÷ d and d = 0.9 ÷ √Ne, the √Ne cancels and the result is 25.4 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 28 for any count.

questions.q: Because 25.4 ÷ d and √Ne both change with count, the maximum cover factor is different for coarse and fine yarns.
questions.explain: The two effects cancel: touching threads per inch is 28.2 √Ne, and dividing by √Ne leaves 28.2 for every count.

questions.q: Tex is converted from Ne using
questions.explain: tex = 590.5 ÷ Ne; for Ne 20 that is 29.5 tex, the worksheet's figure. Multiplying would make finer yarns heavier.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Diameters, touching thread counts and cover limits computed from the lecture's formulas.

questions.q: Using d (mm) = 0.9 ÷ √Ne, what is the diameter of an Ne 36 yarn? Give three decimals.
Convert Ne 10 to tex (tex = 590.5 ÷ Ne). Give one decimal.
Using d (mm) = √tex ÷ 26.7, what is the diameter of a 100 tex yarn? Give three decimals.
An Ne 36 yarn has a diameter of 0.150 mm. How many such yarns lie touching in one inch (25.4 mm)? Give one decimal.
questions.explain: 25.4 ÷ 0.150 = 169.3 threads per inch.

questions.q: If 169.3 Ne 36 yarns fill an inch when touching, what is the maximum cover factor per direction (threads per inch ÷ √Ne)? Give one decimal.
questions.explain: 169.3 ÷ 6 = 28.2, the same ceiling the lecture finds for Ne 20.

questions.q: An Ne 60 yarn: find its diameter from 0.9 ÷ √Ne and then the touching threads per inch (25.4 ÷ d). Give the threads per inch to one decimal.
One metre of a 29.53 tex yarn with specific volume 1.1 cm³/g occupies what volume? Give it in cm³ to four decimals.
Using the full formula d (cm) = √(4 v N ÷ (1000 π l)) with v = 1.0 cm³/g, N = 29.53 tex and l = 100 cm, what is the diameter in mm? Give three decimals.
questions.explain: 4 × 1.0 × 29.53 ÷ (1000 × π × 100) = 3.76 × 10⁻⁴; the square root is 0.01939 cm = 0.194 mm, about 5 % less than the 0.203 mm found with v = 1.1.

questions.q: The worksheet gives 0.144 mm for an Ne 40 yarn. Which Ne count would have a diameter of about 0.10 mm by the 0.9 ÷ √Ne rule?
questions.explain: 0.9 ÷ √Ne = 0.10 gives √Ne = 9, so Ne = 81. Ne 100 would give 0.09 mm and Ne 60 about 0.116 mm.

questions.q: A 36 tex yarn has d = √36 ÷ 26.7 mm. To the nearest 0.001 mm this is
questions.explain: √36 = 6 and 6 ÷ 26.7 = 0.225 mm. 0.449 would result from forgetting the square root in a different way (12 ÷ 26.7), and 0.135 from using 36 ÷ 26.7 ÷ 10.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Using the diameter estimate in the design office: setts, cover limits, yarn substitutions and the limits of the model.

questions.q: A designer proposes 140 ends per inch of Ne 20 yarn. Is this feasible by the lecture's model?
options: No, because only about 126 Ne 20 yarns fit touching in an inch
Yes, if the weft is finer
questions.explain: The worksheet shows 126 Ne 20 yarns (0.2 mm each) fill an inch when touching; 140 would exceed the geometric limit even before any weave interlacing is allowed for.

questions.q: A mill replaces an Ne 20 warp with Ne 30 at the same ends per inch. The cover factor
options: Rises, because the yarn is thinner
Falls, because the yarn is thinner and leaves more space
questions.explain: Cover factor = EPI ÷ √Ne; with EPI fixed and Ne up from 20 to 30 the cover falls, matching the thinner yarn (0.166 mm against 0.203 mm) covering less of the cloth.

questions.q: A costing office needs a yarn diameter quickly but has only the Ne count. Which rule should it use?
questions.explain: The Ne form is 0.9 ÷ √Ne; √tex ÷ 26.7 needs the count in tex first. The other two are not diameter formulas at all.

questions.q: If a cloth is woven with warp cover factor 28, the lecture's model says the warp yarns are essentially touching.
questions.explain: 28 is the cover factor at which the touching-yarn count (25.4 ÷ d) is reached, so there is no space left between the warp yarns.

questions.q: A lab measures real cotton yarns in a cloth and finds they cover more area than the formula predicts. The lecture's explanation is
options: The yarns are flattened at the interlacings, so they are wider than the circular model
The specific volume should be higher than 1.1
The formula only works for polyester
questions.explain: The lecture notes that real cotton yarns in cloth are flattened and cover more than the circular model predicts; the model is an estimate, not a measurement.

questions.q: A spinner supplies a bulkier open-end yarn with specific volume nearer 1.3 cm³/g instead of 1.1. For the same count the yarn will be
options: Thinner, so the sett can be raised
Thicker, so fewer threads fit per inch
questions.explain: Diameter rises with √v, so the bulkier yarn is thicker and fewer touching threads fit in an inch. Weight per metre is fixed by the count, not the bulk.

questions.q: Two yarns are compared: 30 tex and 15 tex. In a cloth with the same thread spacing, the 15 tex yarn
options: Takes half the width of the 30 tex yarn
Takes about 71 % of the width of the 30 tex yarn
Takes a quarter of the width
questions.explain: Diameter ∝ √tex, so halving the tex multiplies the width by √0.5 ≈ 0.71, not 0.5.

questions.q: A planner reads a worksheet value of 154.6 touching threads per inch for Ne 30. What does this number represent?
options: The geometric maximum ends per inch if the yarns are packed side by side with no gaps
The picks per inch in plain weave
questions.explain: It is 25.4 ÷ d — a ceiling, not a recommendation; real setts are lower to leave room for the interlacing of the other set of threads.

questions.q: The yarn-diameter model can be used to check whether a proposed sett is physically possible before a loom trial is run.
questions.explain: Comparing the proposed threads per inch with 25.4 ÷ d shows at once whether the yarns could even fit, saving a wasted trial.

questions.q: A merchandiser quotes a yarn as 0.9 mm in diameter because it is Ne 1. Is the figure consistent with the lecture's formula?
options: The formula cannot be used below Ne 10
questions.explain: 0.9 ÷ √1 = 0.9 mm; the formula applies for any count, though such a coarse yarn is unusual in cotton cloth.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder reasoning across the derivation, the constants and the limits of the cylinder model.

questions.q: Starting from mass × v = π d² l ÷ 4 for one metre of N tex yarn, which expression for d is correct (cm units)?
questions.explain: Mass is N ÷ 1000 g, volume N v ÷ 1000 cm³; equate to π d² l ÷ 4 and solve: d² = 4 N v ÷ (1000 π l). Option C is its reciprocal and B forgets the square root.

questions.q: Compute the constant in d (mm) = √tex ÷ k for v = 1.1 cm³/g and l = 100 cm: k = 1 ÷ (10 × √(4 × 1.1 ÷ (1000 × π × 100))). Give one decimal.
A student computes d for Ne 20 as √20 ÷ 26.7 = 0.167 mm. What went wrong?
options: The √tex formula was used with an Ne count; Ne 20 is 29.5 tex, giving 0.203 mm
The answer should be in inches
questions.explain: The 26.7 constant belongs to tex. Ne 20 must first be converted (590.5 ÷ 20 = 29.5 tex), after which √29.5 ÷ 26.7 = 0.203 mm.

questions.q: The maximum cover factor per direction is 25.4 ÷ 0.9 for any count. Give it to one decimal.
questions.explain: 25.4 ÷ 0.9 = 28.2; the count cancels because touching threads per inch = 28.2 √Ne and cover factor divides by √Ne.

questions.q: Doubling the specific volume of a yarn doubles its diameter.
questions.explain: Diameter varies with the square root of specific volume, so doubling v raises d by √2 ≈ 1.41, not 2.

questions.q: A square plain cloth is woven from Ne 20 yarn (d = 0.2 mm) at 63 ends per inch. What fraction of the touching-thread limit of 126 per inch is used? Give it to two decimals.
questions.explain: 63 ÷ 126 = 0.50: the warp uses half the available width, leaving the other half for the weft to pass through.

questions.q: Why is a cover factor of 28 in both warp and weft impossible in a real plain weave?
options: Because both sets of threads would need the whole area, leaving no space for one to pass over and under the other
Because the reed cannot be made fine enough
questions.explain: 28 in one direction already fills the inch with touching yarns; the other set of threads needs room to interlace between them, so the combined cover must stay well below 28 + 28.

questions.q: The worksheet gives 0.144 mm for Ne 40 from specific volume but 0.142 mm from 0.9 ÷ √Ne. Which is the more exact value for v = 1.1, and why?
options: 0.144 mm, because it is computed from the full formula while 0.9 is a rounded constant
0.142 mm, because Ne formulas are always more accurate
Neither, the true value is 0.164 mm
questions.explain: The specific-volume row uses the derivation directly; 0.9 ÷ √Ne is a convenient approximation with a rounded constant. 0.164 mm is the Ne 30 yarn.

questions.q: Convert the diameter of an Ne 16 yarn to inches using d (in) ≈ 1 ÷ (28 √Ne). Give four decimals.
Which of these would NOT change the diameter predicted by the cylinder model?
options: Changing the weave the yarn is used in
Converting from Ne to tex before calculating
questions.explain: The model uses only count and specific volume; the weave affects how the yarn is flattened in the cloth, which the circular model ignores. Converting Ne to tex correctly gives the same diameter.
